title: User Account Control
summary: User Account Control, usually shortened to UAC, is the Windows feature that keeps a session running with standard user rights and asks for explicit approval before an action needs administrator rights. Even when you sign in with an administrator account, Windows gives your programs a filtered token, so a routine task such as opening a document cannot silently change system settings. When elevation is required, the consent prompt appears and, on the secure desktop setting, the screen dims so a normal process cannot draw a fake prompt over it. In real environments the relevant decisions are the consent prompt behaviour for administrators, the credential prompt for standard users, and whether prompts land on the secure desktop. Evidence appears in the security event log, where approval and request events record which program asked to elevate, which account approved it, and whether the request succeeded.

beginner.definition: User Account Control is a Windows safety feature. It asks you to confirm before a program makes a big change to the computer. It also means your everyday programs run with normal user rights, not full control. Only the action that truly needs more power gets more power.
beginner.whyItMatters: If every program ran with full control, one bad click could change system files or install software. Attackers rely on that, because it lets them turn a small mistake into control of the whole machine. User Account Control puts a step in the middle, so a quiet change becomes a visible question. It also creates a record of who approved what. Ignoring or switching off those prompts removes that step completely.
howItWorks: Windows gives your session a limited set of rights, even when you sign in as an administrator.
When a task needs administrator rights, the system pauses it and prepares a prompt.
Windows fades the screen and shows the prompt on a separate secure desktop. Normal programs cannot draw on it.
An administrator clicks yes, or a standard user types an administrator password instead.
The system records the request, the program name and the decision in its security log.
If the user says no, or the request fails, the program keeps running without the extra rights.
beginner.example: Imagine an office building where everyone can enter their own floor with a simple key. The server room needs a different key, and the front desk asks you what you need before handing it over. The desk keeps a written record of every time that key leaves the drawer. A patient attacker would need to fool the person at the desk, in public, with their name written down.
takeaways: Leave User Account Control on and keep the prompt on the secure desktop.
Teach people to read the prompt instead of clicking yes by habit, because that habit is the weakness.
The approval log is useful evidence when you investigate how a change happened.

objectives: Describe how User Account Control separates everyday work from administrator actions on Windows.
Explain the difference between the consent prompt and the credential prompt.
Justify why running daily work as a standard user reduces risk.
Locate the Windows security events that record elevation requests and approvals.
Identify risky UAC configurations and the behaviour they enable.
